questions.q: What problem does exponential backoff primarily solve?
options: It guarantees each retry eventually succeeds
It reduces the latency of individual requests
Growing waits ease pressure on a struggling dependency
It prioritizes premium traffic over background jobs during recovery

questions.q: Why add jitter to retry delays?
options: Random delays desynchronize clients so retries don't arrive in waves
Jitter shortens the average wait between attempts
Jitter hides timing information from network attackers
Jitter guarantees perfectly fair scheduling between competing clients under load

questions.q: In which circuit breaker state are calls rejected instantly without reaching the dependency?
options: Closed
Half-open
Tripped-idle
Open

questions.q: What happens in a circuit breaker's half-open state?
options: All requests queue until a recovery timer expires
A few probes pass through; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it
Requests fail fast while errors are logged for review
Traffic is duplicated to a standby replica so both paths can be compared live

questions.q: Why must every remote call carry an explicit timeout?
options: Stalled calls otherwise pin threads and connections, cascading the failure
Timeouts materially reduce median response latency
TCP connections cannot detect any failures on their own
Load balancers silently drop any connection that does not advertise timeout headers

questions.q: Which response is generally worth retrying automatically?
options: 400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
503 Service Unavailable
404 Not Found

questions.q: Safely retrying a write generally requires what?
options: TLS on every hop of the request path
The operation to be idempotent or deduplicated server-side
Retry intervals of at least one second
Routing the write through a durable message queue before it executes

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a circuit breaker?
options: Retrying failed calls with smarter scheduling
Balancing traffic away from slow replicas
Caching the most recent successful response for reuse throughout an outage window
Failing fast and shielding a failing dependency so it can recover

questions.q: Three call layers each retry 3 times on failure. Worst-case attempts hitting the bottom layer?
What does a retry budget, say retries capped at 10% of requests, protect against?
options: Slow clients starving fast ones at the balancer
Retries amplifying an outage into self-inflicted overload
Clock skew corrupting backoff computations across many hosts
Uneven shard traffic during rebalancing events

questions.q: Retries run at the client, the gateway, and the service layer, and small blips become outages. Best remedy?
options: Retry at a single layer under a budget; the others fail fast
Raise all timeouts so each layer's retries have enough room to finish
Add database-layer retries so every tier behaves consistently
Replace exponential backoff with fixed one-second delays

questions.q: Service A calls B with a 2s timeout; B calls C with a 5s timeout. What is wrong?
options: C will reject the call for exceeding its own deadline
B's connection pool leaks one socket on every request until it exhausts file handles
A gives up at 2s while C keeps working — inner timeouts must be shorter
Nothing — hop timeouts are independent by design

questions.q: What is the practical risk of exponential backoff with no maximum cap?
options: Retries re-synchronize into coordinated waves after several doubling rounds complete
Delays grow so long that clients effectively never recover after extended incidents
The arithmetic overflows and crashes most standard libraries
Throughput exceeds intended limits once the service heals

questions.q: A breaker trips after 2 consecutive failures and flaps constantly on a low-traffic service. Better trigger?
options: Trip on any single 5xx response
Trip on the first timeout only
Disable the breaker entirely during quiet hours when traffic is naturally low
An error-rate threshold with a minimum request volume per window

questions.q: How does AWS-style 'full jitter' choose a retry delay?
options: Base delay plus a fixed ten percent random bump
The exponential delay minus a constant jitter term
Uniform random between zero and the current exponential cap
A Gaussian sample centered on the base delay

questions.q: A dependency is down, so the caller queues incoming requests to replay later. Likely outcome?
options: Unbounded queue growth, memory pressure, then serving long-stale work
Graceful recovery once the dependency returns
Lower tail latency because the queue smooths bursts into a steady drain rate
Automatic deduplication of the queued requests

questions.q: One slow endpoint trips a breaker shared across all of a dependency's endpoints. Consequence?
options: Healthy endpoints get blocked too — scope breakers per endpoint or operation
The slow endpoint recovers faster because reduced pressure reaches it before the others
Retry storms concentrate on the remaining endpoints
Nothing — breakers are always per-endpoint by default

questions.q: Latency rises near capacity; clients time out and retry; overload persists even after the trigger clears. Why?
options: TCP slow start throttles all recovering connections
DNS caching keeps every client pinned to the sickest host
Retry load keeps the system saturated — a metastable failure state
Circuit breakers hold open until manually reset

questions.q: What does deadline propagation add beyond per-hop timeouts?
options: Longer effective timeouts for deep call chains
Per-hop encryption of timing metadata
Automatic retry scheduling at each downstream hop without client involvement
Downstream work is abandoned once the caller's overall budget is spent

questions.q: After a long outage the dependency returns, thousands of breakers half-open at once, and it collapses again. Mitigation?
options: Shorten the open duration so probes start sooner
Stagger probe timing with jitter and ramp traffic up gradually
Send more probes per breaker to confirm health faster
Close every breaker immediately on the first success signal seen anywhere
